nameStory: The Eastern Water Shrew gets its name from its amazing ability to literally walk on water! Unlike other shrews that stick to dry land, this tiny mammal has evolved special adaptations that let it hunt for food both underwater and on the water's surface. The 'eastern' part simply tells us which side of North America it calls home.
description: The Eastern Water Shrew is one of New England's most remarkable but rarely seen mammals - a mouse-sized creature that's actually more closely related to moles than to mice. These tiny hunters measure just 5-6 inches long including their tail, weighing less than half an ounce. They have velvety dark fur, a long pointed snout, and incredibly small eyes, perfectly designed for their aquatic lifestyle. Think of them as nature's tiniest otters!

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Smaller than a house mouse with a long, flexible snout that feels almost rubbery to the touch. The body is compact and torpedo-shaped, built for swimming through water and darting through streamside vegetation.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dense, velvety fur that feels incredibly soft and appears almost black when wet, silvery-gray when dry. The fur has a water-repelling quality that makes droplets bead up and roll off - you can actually see air bubbles trapped in the fur underwater.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny star-shaped prints in soft mud near water, with five delicate toes spreading outward. Look for paired tracks leading directly to and from water's edge - they rarely wander far from streams.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: The telltale behavior is seeing a small dark shape literally running across the water surface or diving underwater near rocky streams. They move in quick, jerky motions and can stay submerged for several seconds while hunting.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found within a few feet of clean, cold, fast-moving water. Look for them near rocky stream edges where you can hear water bubbling over stones - they need the oxygen-rich environment.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Tiny food caches of aquatic insects and larvae hidden under overhanging rocks near water. Their scat is incredibly small and hard to spot, but disturbed areas in streamside leaf litter can indicate their presence.

habitat: Eastern Water Shrews live along clean, cold mountain streams and rocky brooks throughout New England's forested regions, particularly at higher elevations. They prefer areas where clear water flows over rocky bottoms, creating the oxygen-rich environment they need. You'll find them near stream banks with plenty of overhanging vegetation and moss-covered rocks that provide cover.

seasonality.spring: Most active as streams swell with snowmelt, providing abundant aquatic prey. This is peak breeding season when you're most likely to spot their water-walking behavior.
seasonality.summer: Continue hunting in streams but may be harder to spot during hot days when they rest under cool, damp rocks. Early morning and evening offer best viewing opportunities.
seasonality.fall: Building up fat reserves for winter, they're very active and easier to observe. Their dark fur becomes thicker and more luxurious in preparation for cold weather.
seasonality.winter: Remain active under ice and snow, creating tunnel systems in streamside banks. Look for small holes in snow near unfrozen stream sections where they emerge to hunt.

funFact: Eastern Water Shrews can literally walk on water thanks to tiny air bubbles trapped in their fur and fringed hairs on their feet that work like snowshoes - they're so light and quick that surface tension holds them up, making them look like furry water striders!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young mice or voles near water, but shrews have that distinctive long, pointed snout and much smaller eyes. Remember: if it's running ON the water rather than swimming through it, you've found your water shrew!
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 confirmed sightings in New England, the Eastern Water Shrew is one of our region's rarest mammals - spotting one would be like finding a needle in a haystack! Many naturalists go their entire careers without seeing one, making any sighting truly special and worth reporting to local wildlife authorities.
compareHints: Unlike the Masked Shrew which stays on dry land, the Eastern Water Shrew is always found near water and has denser, more water-repellent fur. The Smoky Shrew is larger and grayer, while the tiny Pygmy Shrew is much smaller and lacks any aquatic adaptations. If you see a shrew near water that can actually swim and dive, you've likely found the rare Eastern Water Shrew.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Masked shrews are smaller and grayer than the reddish-brown smoky shrew, and much larger than the tiny American pygmy shrew.
Compared to its relatives, the smoky shrew is larger than both the tiny masked shrew and the even tinier American pygmy shrew, and it lacks the specialized swimming adaptations of the water shrew.

Compared to its closest relatives, the American pygmy shrew is noticeably smaller than both the masked shrew and smoky shrew, and lacks the distinctive white belly markings of the eastern water shrew.
